props.title: A Canterbury Tale

sections.content: A Canterbury Tale (1944) stands as one of Powell and Pressburger's most enigmatic masterpieces, blending wartime reality with mystical elements that echo Chaucer's medieval pilgrims. The film follows three modern "pilgrims" - a British soldier, an American GI, and a land girl - who converge in the fictional Kent town of Chillingbourne. Like I Know Where I'm Going! (1945) and The Edge of the World (1937), it explores the tension between tradition and progress, rural and urban life. The film's mysterious "glue man" who pours glue into women's hair becomes a strange catalyst for examining English heritage during wartime.

movies.title: I Know Where I'm Going!
movies.slug: A headstrong woman's planned marriage is disrupted by Scottish Highland magic and romance

sections.content: The film's unusual structure mirrors wartime Britain's disorientation. Like Brief Encounter (1945) and Millions Like Us (1943), it captures the home front's strange mixture of ancient traditions and modern warfare. But while those films stay grounded in realism, A Canterbury Tale ventures into almost supernatural territory. The medieval past bleeds into the present through Thomas Colpeper, the village magistrate who connects directly to England's deep history while acting as an unlikely guardian of traditional values. SUBHEAD: Wartime British Cinema's Spiritual Turn

This film represents a unique strand of 1940s British cinema that sought spiritual meaning amid warfare. While In Which We Serve (1942) and The Way Ahead (1944) focused on military heroism, Powell and Pressburger explored mystical connections to landscape and history. Their later A Matter of Life and Death (1946) would push even further into supernatural territory, but A Canterbury Tale remains their most grounded fusion of the magical and mundane.
